orders.description: Plaintiffs’ and ABM’s limited appeals from the single July 28, 2022 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied ABM dismissal; granted dismissal to owner NYP and managers CBRE.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on a shelf detached from a collapsed shelving unit while working for JPMorgan in NYP’s office building. CBRE managed the building and ABM provided janitorial services; ABM’s porter allegedly pulled a shelf just before or during collapse.

legal_issues.finding: NYP lacked relevant repair/maintenance duty and CBRE owed plaintiff no duty on this record; ABM’s potential creation-based duty remained triable.
ABM porter’s pulling raised an issue of launching an instrument of harm. CBRE established it did not assemble the unit; plaintiff’s speculative testimony did not implicate CBRE.
NYP established out-of-possession status with no relevant maintenance obligation. Limited cleaning duties did not cover the pleaded accident; prior notice alone would not impose liability.
Espinal creation exception remained triable for ABM but not CBRE. ABM was an independent contractor, not NYP/CBRE’s agent; general supervision did not establish vicarious liability.
Court declined to search record for ABM cross-claim relief and denied motion to strike part of record/briefs.
NYP/CBRE could not be held vicariously liable for independent contractor ABM on mere general supervision; NYP also could not be liable through CBRE’s alleged negligence.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s testimony about assembly was speculative and did not implicate CBRE.

quality.notes: All appealed portions affirmed: different underlying outcomes for defendants are not a mixed appellate result. Favors both reflects surviving ABM claim and other dismissals. One appealed order; strike motion ancillary. Explicit personal slip on detached shelf, not merely an object striking plaintiff. No date, detailed contract document or statutory violation inferred. Unchanged rules for 2023 opinion.

evidence.quote: Nervo, J.), entered on or about July 28, 2022, which, to the extent appealed from as limited by the briefs, denied defendant ABM Facility Services' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint as against it and granted defendants 4 NYP Ventures LLC, CB Richard Ellis Real Estate Services, LLC, and CBRE Group, Inc.'s motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint as against them, unanimously affirmed, without costs.

Plaintiff Douglas Caldwell allegedly sustained injuries when he slipped and fell on a shelf that detached from a collapsed shelving unit while working for third-party defendant JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A. (JPMorgan) in an office building owned by defendant third-party plaintiff 4 NYP Ventures LLC (NYP). Defendants CB Richard Ellis Real Estate Services, LLC and CBRE Group, Inc. (together, CBRE) managed the building and defendant ABM Facility Services (ABM) provided janitorial services at the building.
The court correctly determined that an issue of fact existed as to whether ABM's porter launched an instrument of harm by pulling on a shelf in the shelving unit just before or while it collapsed

The court correctly determined that the record evidence establishes, as a matter of law, that CBRE did not assemble the shelving unit that collapsed and thus, CBRE did not launch an instrument of harm ( see Espinal , 98 NY2d at 140). Plaintiff's testimony regarding who assembled the shelving unit does not raise a triable issue of fact because it is speculative and does not implicate CBRE. The court also correctly determined that the record evidence also establishes, as a matter of law, that ABM was an independent contractor rather than an agent of CBRE or NYP

The record evidence shows, at most, that NYP and CBRE retained general supervisory powers over ABM, which are insufficient to support vicarious liability ( e.g. Melbourne , 271 AD2d at 297; see also Matter of Yoga Vida NYC, Inc. [Commissioner of Labor] , 28 NY3d 1013 , 1016 [2016]). Thus, plaintiff cannot hold NYP or CBRE vicariously liable for ABM's alleged negligence.

The court correctly determined that the record evidence establishes, as a matter of law, that NYP was an out-of-possession landlord that did not have any relevant contractual obligation to repair or maintain the premises ( see Padilla [*2] v Holrod Assoc. LLC , 215 AD3d 573 , 573 [1st Dept 2023]). Although NYP had a contractual obligation to clean certain portions of the office building, plaintiffs do not contend that the accident was caused by negligent cleaning or a significant structural or design defect that is contrary to a specific statutory safety provision.

To the extent the plaintiff argues that NYP had prior notice of the defective condition, "[a]n out of possession landlord may not be held liable even if it had notice of the defective condition prior to the accident" ( Padilla , 215 AD3d at 574). Plaintiffs cannot maintain their claims against NYP premised on vicarious liability for CBRE or ABM's alleged negligence because as discussed above, CBRE owed no duty to plaintiff and ABM was an independent contractor.
We decline ABM's invitation to search the record and grant it summary judgment on certain cross-claims ( see CPLR 3212 [b]).
Motion to strike portion of the record and certain respondents' briefs denied.

orders.description: Plaintiffs’ appeal from the March 31, 2016 order.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped over an exposed tree root in the common side yard beside the condominium unit she leased with her husband. Defendants owned and managed the complex.

legal_issues.finding: No duty to protect/warn against this obvious condition inherent or incidental to the property and reasonably anticipated by users.
Root was open/obvious, inherent or incidental to this property, and previously known to plaintiff; opposition raised no issue.

quality.notes: Owned condominium common yard supports private status; no sidewalk boundary issue. Tree root is obstruction; no raised pavement inferred. No date or evidence format supplied. Inherent/incidental condition is the court’s rationale, not a recreational assumption-of-risk holding.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff Jennifer Commender (hereinafter the injured plaintiff) allegedly tripped and fell over an exposed tree root in a common area located in the side yard next to a condominium unit that she leased with her husband.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the plaintiffs appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Asher, J.), dated March 31, 2016, which granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
The injured plaintiff, and her husband suing derivatively, commenced this action against the defendants, the owner and manager of the condominium complex.

Here, the defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the complaint by demonstrating that the tree root was an open and obvious condition and inherent or incidental to the nature of the property, and was known to the injured [*2] plaintiff prior to the accident ( see Dottavio v Aspen Knolls Estates Home Owners Assn. , 147 AD3d 910 , 911 [2017]; Badalbaeva v City of New York , 55 AD3d 764 , 764-765 [2008]; Torres v State of New York , 18 AD3d 739 , 739 [2005]; Mazzola v Mazzola , 16 AD3d 629 , 630 [2005]). In opposition, the plaintiffs failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiffs’ appeal from the August 20, 2012 order.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped on an outdoor patio at defendant’s owned/operated restaurant. Although she could not identify the cause, eyewitness testimony and photographs taken almost immediately afterward showed the cracked patio condition in the incident area.

legal_issues.finding: Plaintiff’s deposition initially established inability to identify cause, but eyewitness deposition and contemporaneous photographs raised a triable issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant submitted injured plaintiff’s deposition acknowledging inability to identify cause.
Opposing eyewitness deposition, considered with photographs, raised a factual issue.
Photos taken almost immediately after fall showed patio cracks in incident area.

quality.notes: Outdoor patio is other location. Cracked condition is evidentiary support, not finally determined cause or negligent defect. No customer/guest role, accident date or notice finding inferred.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.

Bianca Mottola (hereinafter the injured plaintiff), and her husband suing derivatively, commenced this action to recover damages for injuries allegedly sustained when the injured plaintiff tripped and fell on the outdoor patio at a restaurant owned and operated by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the plaintiffs appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (Tolbert, J.), entered August 20, 2012, which granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendant established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by its submission of the transcript of the injured plaintiff's deposition, at which the injured plaintiff testified that she was unable to identify the cause of her fall

In opposition to the motion, however, the plaintiffs raised a triable issue of fact through the deposition testimony of an eyewitness, together with photographs taken almost immediately after the injured plaintiff fell, showing the cracked condition of the patio floor in the area of the incident
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Wal-Mart defendants’ limited appeal from the September 23, 2014 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied complaint-dismissal branch against Wal-Mart defendants.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on a wet spot near an ice machine at the front of defendants’ owned/operated store. Employees traversed and monitored the area minutes before the fall; neither they nor plaintiff reported seeing water beforehand.

legal_issues.finding: Plaintiffs’ claim of a triable creation issue was rejected without separate factual explanation.
Wal-Mart established no prior advice or written/oral complaints about floor water or machine leaks; plaintiffs raised no issue.
Employee affidavits and surveillance showed actual monitoring minutes before the accident, with no observed water. Wetness was not shown visible/apparent long enough for discovery and remedy.
Plaintiffs’ contention that the appeal was frivolous was rejected.

evidence_discussed.description: Employee affidavits described monitoring on the accident day and no observed water.
Surveillance recordings showed employees walking through and monitoring the accident area minutes beforehand.
Plaintiff’s deposition stated she had not seen wetness a few minutes before falling.

quality.notes: Annotate supplied 2016 ruling only, without importing later appellate history or cited-case labels. Ice-machine proximity does not establish a leak. Actual inspection evidence distinguished from general practices. No injured role/date inferred.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with costs, and the appellants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them is granted.

The plaintiff Dolores Parietti (hereinafter the injured plaintiff) allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on a wet spot on the floor near an ice machine inside the front of a store owned and operated by the defendants Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., and Wal-Mart Stores East, L.P. (hereinafter together Wal-Mart).

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the defendants Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., and Wal-Mart Stores East, L.P., appeal from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Pitts, J.), dated September 23, 2014, as denied that branch of their motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them.

Here, Wal-Mart established, prima facie, that it did not have actual notice of the wet condition of the floor. Wal-Mart submitted evidence in support of its motion which demonstrated that it was not advised of the wet condition on the floor and it did not receive any written or oral complaints by customers or employees concerning water on the floor or a leak in the ice machine prior to the accident

While the evidence submitted in support of the motion demonstrated that water may have been present on the floor where the injured plaintiff fell, Wal-Mart established that the alleged wet condition did not exist for a sufficient length of time prior to the accident such that its employees were able to discover and remedy it. Employee affidavits and video surveillance recordings submitted by Wal-Mart demonstrated that its employees, as per protocol, monitored the conditions at the front entrance of the store on the date of the accident and walked back and forth in the area where the injured plaintiff fell only minutes before her accident. None of the employees at the front of the store saw any water on the floor prior to the injured plaintiff's accident. Even the injured plaintiff testified at her deposition that she did not see the alleged wet condition a few minutes prior to her accident.

In opposition, the plaintiffs failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether Wal-Mart had actual or constructive notice of the wet condition ( see Zuckerman v City of New York , 49 NY2d 557, 562 [1980]). To the extent that the plaintiffs argue that there is a triable issue as to whether Wal-Mart created the hazard, the argument is without merit. The plaintiffs' remaining contention, that Wal-Mart's appeal is frivolous, is without merit.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted Wal-Mart's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

orders.description: Plaintiffs’ appeal No. 2 from the June 28, 2019 amended order.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted contractor’s dismissal motion and owners’ dismissal cross motion; denied plaintiffs’ summary-judgment cross motion.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on ice in a parking lot owned by the Benderson defendants, who hired Ridge for snow removal. Plaintiff described conditions at the scene; the parties submitted competing meteorologist affidavits.

legal_issues.finding: Owners and snow-removal contractor established suspension of removal duty during storm and reasonable time afterward; possible lull did not create adequate time.
Plaintiffs failed to raise an issue of a causal preexisting condition with defendants’ actual or constructive notice; categories not separately conclusively found.
Plaintiffs failed to raise an issue of a causal preexisting condition with defendants’ actual or constructive notice; categories not separately conclusively found.

Defendants’ expert established an ongoing storm. Plaintiff’s observations showed at most a lull without reasonable remediation time; preexisting-condition/notice and opposing expert theories raised no issue.
Defense expert’s local weather account established the defense; plaintiffs’ expert was speculative/conclusory on regional weather, preexisting ice and storm timing.

evidence_discussed.description: Both sides submitted meteorologist affidavits; defense detailed local conditions, opposing opinion deemed speculative.
Plaintiff’s deposition observations showed at most a possible lull/break, not sufficient cleanup time.

quality.notes: Private lot ownership express. One amended order; Appeal No. 2 is a source identifier, not proof of a second disposition in this opinion. No other appeal consulted or merged. No independent Espinal issue, weather-record format, date or injured role inferred. Unchanged rules for 2021 opinion.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the amended order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.

Plaintiffs commenced this action seeking damages for injuries sustained by Glenn Gould (plaintiff) when he allegedly slipped and fell on ice in a parking lot on property owned by defendants 93 NYRPT, LLC and Ronald Benderson 1995 Trust (collectively, Benderson defendants). The Benderson defendants contracted with defendant Ridge Maintenance Corp. (Ridge) to perform snow removal at the property.

Appeal from an amended order of the Supreme Court, Erie County (Emilio L. Colaiacovo, J.), entered June 28, 2019. The amended order granted the motion of defendant Ridge Maintenance Corp. and the cross motion of defendants 93 NYRPT, LLC and Ronald Benderson 1995 Trust for summary judgment dismissing the complaint and denied the cross motion of plaintiffs for summary judgment.

Contrary to plaintiffs' contention, we conclude that defendants met their respective initial burdens on their motion and cross motion for summary judgment. Defendants submitted the affidavit of an expert meteorologist, which detailed the weather conditions in the area where the slip and fall occurred and thereby established that "a storm was in progress at the time of the [slip and fall] and, thus, that [defendants] had no duty to remove the snow and ice until a reasonable time ha[d] elapsed after cessation of the storm"

Although defendants also submitted the deposition testimony of plaintiff stating his observations of the conditions at the scene of the slip and fall, that testimony established, at most, a possible lull or break in the storm that did not [*2] afford defendants a reasonable amount of time in which to correct the hazardous conditions ( see Witherspoon v Tops Mkts., LLC , 128 AD3d 1541 , 1542 [4th Dept 2015]; Gilbert , 124 AD3d at 1327; Baia v Allright Parking Buffalo, Inc. , 27 AD3d 1153 , 1153-1154 [4th Dept 2006]). We further conclude that, in opposition, plaintiffs failed to "raise a triable issue of fact whether the accident was caused by a slippery condition at the location where the plaintiff fell that existed prior to the storm, as opposed to precipitation from the storm in progress, and that the defendant[s] had actual or constructive notice of the preexisting condition"

The opinions contained in the affidavit of the meteorological expert submitted by plaintiffs constitute "mere speculation based on general weather conditions that were prevailing in the region" ( Greco v Grande , 160 AD3d 1345 , 1346 [4th Dept 2018]). The affidavit is also conclusory and speculative with respect to whether the ice existed prior to the storm and whether there was a storm in progress. It is therefore insufficient to raise a triable issue of fact
